title: Month 6
subtitle: Food starts this month. It is messy, it is slow, and almost none of it is about nutrition yet.

baby.development: Most babies can sit with support and are starting to reach and grab. The tongue-thrust reflex fades, which is what makes swallowing possible. Teeth may be arriving.

you.body: If you are breastfeeding, your supply is established and may feel less full. That is normal and not a sign it is dropping.
you.mind: Starting solids is the first place where other people's opinions arrive in force. Pick a lane and ignore the noise.

coreActions.title: Start solids, one food at a time
coreActions.why: Around six months, milk alone stops being enough for iron. The first foods matter less than the fact that you start.
coreActions.detail: Start with iron-rich foods — pureed meat, beans, or iron-fortified cereal. One new food every few days so you can spot a reaction. Milk stays the main source of nutrition until about 12 months; food is practice. No honey before 12 months, no cow's milk as a drink before 12 months, no juice before 12 months, and nothing round and hard.

options.label: Spoon-fed purees
options.detail: Easier to control, less mess, and a fine choice.

options.label: Baby-led weaning
options.detail: Soft finger foods the baby feeds themselves. More mess, more control for the baby.

options.label: Both
options.detail: Most families end up here. There is no rule against it.

coreActions.skipIf: Your pediatrician has recommended a different start date for a medical reason.

coreActions.title: Get a high chair that is easy to clean
coreActions.why: You will use it three times a day for two years. The only features that matter are a footrest, a five-point harness, and a tray that goes in the dishwasher.
coreActions.detail: A footrest matters more than it sounds — a baby whose feet dangle cannot sit stably, and unstable sitting makes eating harder. Avoid anything with fabric you cannot wipe. Do not use a hook-on seat until the baby can sit fully independently.

options.label: IKEA Antilop
options.detail: About $25, wipes clean, footrest available separately. The default answer.

options.label: Stokke Tripp Trapp
options.detail: Expensive, grows with the child, holds resale value.

options.label: A convertible chair
options.detail: Turns into a booster later. Good if space is tight.

coreActions.skipIf: You already have a high chair with a footrest and a harness.

coreActions.title: Start looking for childcare if you need it
coreActions.why: Waitlists in most US cities run six to eighteen months. Six months is the month to get on them, not twelve.
coreActions.detail: Ask three questions of every place: what is the staff-to-child ratio, what is the turnover, and can I visit unannounced. Licensing records are public in every state — look yours up. NAEYC accreditation is a meaningful signal but not the only one.

options.label: A licensed home provider
options.detail: Smaller groups, often cheaper, more flexible.

options.label: A nanny
options.detail: Most expensive, most flexible, and you are the employer.

coreActions.skipIf: You have childcare arranged, or you are not returning to work.

alsoKnow.title: Water
alsoKnow.body: A little water in an open cup with meals is fine from six months. Do not give juice, and do not give water in place of milk.

alsoKnow.title: Allergens
alsoKnow.body: Introduce peanut, egg, dairy, wheat, soy, fish, and sesame early and keep them in the diet. Delaying them increases the risk of allergy, it does not reduce it.

alsoKnow.title: Teeth
alsoKnow.body: Wipe the gums and any teeth with a soft cloth twice a day. First dental visit by the first tooth or the first birthday, whichever comes first.

alsoKnow.title: Sitting
alsoKnow.body: Sitting with support is not sitting independently. Do not leave a baby propped on a bed or sofa.

redFlags.text: Choking — cannot breathe, cough, or make sound
Swelling of the lips or face, hives with trouble breathing
A fever over 100.4°F with unusual sleepiness or a rash
You are having thoughts of harming yourself or the baby

sources.title: When, What, and How to Introduce Solid Foods
